platforms.title: 3 Habits That Are Quietly Worsening Your PMS
platforms.meta_description: Feeling irritable and bloated every month before your period isn't just hormones acting alone. Sodium, caffeine, alcohol, and inactivity all make PMS worse.
platforms.body_html:
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) gets treated as something that just happens to you every month, but three everyday habits measurably make the irritability and bloating worse — and they're not the ones most people assume.

What's Actually Happening Hormonally

In the luteal phase — the days before your period starts — progesterone drops, and along with it, levels of mood-stabilizing neurotransmitters like serotonin tend to dip too, which is part of why irritability and low mood cluster around this time. At the same time, the hormone aldosterone rises and causes the body to retain more sodium and water, which is the mechanism behind premenstrual bloating. That hormonal backdrop is set regardless of what you do, but three habits layered on top of it extend how long the symptoms last and how intense they feel.

Eating the same amount of sodium as usual — soups, stews, and processed food — keeps the water retention aldosterone is already driving going even longer, since sodium pulls water in in proportion to how much of it you eat. Caffeine and alcohol are a separate mechanism: caffeine sharpens the nervous system's reactivity right when serotonin support is already lower, and alcohol disrupts sleep quality, which compounds fatigue and irritability rather than easing them. Staying sedentary because you feel heavy or low-energy is the third factor — inactivity itself is associated with more persistent fatigue and low mood during this window, the opposite of the instinct to rest completely.

3 Changes That Actually Move the Needle

  • Cook with less salt instead of reaching for broth-heavy meals, and add potassium-rich foods like bananas or spinach, which help balance sodium's water-retaining effect.
  • Swap coffee, green tea, and alcohol for caffeine-free herbal tea in the days before your period — this targets both mechanisms at once, since caffeine and alcohol affect mood and sleep through different pathways but both make this window worse.
  • Take a brisk 20-minute walk instead of resting completely — light aerobic activity is one of the few PMS interventions that works against the fatigue directly, rather than just distracting from it.

It's worth knowing how common this actually is: the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) estimates that up to 90 percent of women of reproductive age notice at least one premenstrual symptom, roughly 20 to 30 percent have symptoms consistent enough to meet the criteria for PMS, and about 5 percent meet criteria for the more severe PMDD — so struggling with this isn't a sign that something is unusually wrong with you, but persistent, life-disrupting symptoms are still worth naming specifically rather than pushing through quietly every month.

None of this means you need to overhaul your entire diet or start training for a race — small, specific swaps in the days before your period are what actually change the symptom pattern. If symptoms are still severe enough to disrupt daily life after two full cycles of trying this, that's the point to bring it to a gynecologist rather than keep managing it alone, since more significant premenstrual mood symptoms can sometimes point to premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), which benefits from a different treatment approach.
